title: Study of Living Wall Systems' (LWSs) Support system for improving LWSs Life cycle performance and noise reduction potential
research_question: To investigate the use of ecofriendly living wall systems (LWSs) and their interactions with acoustic support systems (SSs) to develop a cost-effective urban greening strategy, emphasizing noise attenuation that promotes environmental sustainability and human health, by examining factors influencing sound absorption, comparing different SS designs, and evaluating the effect of greenery coverage rates.

participants.description: Not applicable, study focused on material acoustic properties and their performance in a reverberation room, with implications for human health and environmental sustainability.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Wood-plastic composite (WPC) panels (Type A and B) with varying chamber designs, air gaps (none, 2.5 cm, 30 cm), and three perforation patterns (Design 1, 2, 3). These were tested alone and in combination with Jacobaea maritima greenery modules at different coverage rates (0%, 33%, 65%, 100%). A total of 17 WPC boards (247.5 cm x 15 cm each) were used per setup, and 552 greenery systems were applied across 46 cases for greenery setups.

measures.instrument: Reverberation room method (ISO 354-2003, ASTM C423-17) for one-third octave band frequencies of 100–4,000 Hz
Calculated as the average of sound absorption coefficients at 250, 500, 1000, and 2000 Hz

findings.antecedent: WPC Type A panel absorber (A1, 12.93 mm chamber height, 25.65 mm thickness)
findings.mechanism: Chambers within the WPC panel, originally for weight reduction, also contribute to sound absorption.
findings.quote: The noise reduction coefficients (NRC) of A1... were 0.15... First, WPC type A can be viewed as a panel absorber itself

findings.antecedent: WPC Type A with 2.5 cm air gap (A2)
findings.quote: The noise reduction coefficients (NRC) of A1, A2... were 0.15, 0.20...

findings.antecedent: WPC Type A with perforation design 3 (A3)
findings.quote: The noise reduction coefficients (NRC) of A1, A2, A3... were 0.15, 0.20, 0.20...

findings.antecedent: WPC Type A with 2.5 cm air gap and perforation design 1 (A4)
findings.quote: The noise reduction coefficients (NRC) of A1... A4... were 0.15... 0.25...

findings.antecedent: WPC Type A with 2.5 cm air gap and perforation design 2 (A5)
findings.quote: The noise reduction coefficients (NRC) of A1... A5... were 0.15... 0.25...

findings.antecedent: WPC Type A with 2.5 cm air gap and perforation design 3 (A6)
findings.quote: The noise reduction coefficients (NRC) of A1... A6... were 0.15... 0.25...

findings.antecedent: Introducing a 2.5-cm air gap to WPC Type A (A2 vs A1)
findings.quote: A comparison of the A1 and A2 designs reveals that sound absorption increased at frequencies of less than 500 Hz and decreased at frequencies of 500–3,150 Hz

findings.antecedent: Introducing perforation design 3 to WPC Type A (A3 vs A1)
findings.mechanism: Consistent with the theory of the Helmholtz resonator.
findings.quote: A comparison of the A1 and A3 designs revealed a similar trend; sound absorption improved at frequencies below 500 Hz and decreased at higher frequencies

findings.antecedent: Higher perforation rates in WPC Type A (A4-A6)
findings.mechanism: Consistent with the theory of the standing wave tube.
findings.quote: the results for A4-A6 are also consistent with the theory of the standing wave tube; higher perforation rates corresponded to a higher absorption frequency range

findings.antecedent: Different perforation rates in the same chamber (A4 vs A5)
findings.quote: the differences in the A4 and A5 designs... did not result in a significant difference in sound absorption

findings.antecedent: Different perforation rates in different lanes (A5 vs A6)
findings.quote: the A5 and A6 designs... exhibited significant differences in absorption

findings.antecedent: WPC Type A (A1, higher density) vs WPC Type B (B1, lower density)
findings.mechanism: Specimen weight is the dominant factor for panel absorber mechanism at low frequencies.
findings.quote: A1 still exhibited better sound absorption than B1 overall even B1 had slightly higher chamber height... the dominate factor should be the specimens' weight.

findings.antecedent: Grooved surface pattern (B2) vs non-grooved surface (B1) on WPC Type B
findings.mechanism: Grooved pattern provides better sound scatter, diffraction, and reflection ability at higher frequencies.
findings.quote: The grooved surface of B2 performed slightly better than that of B1 at sound frequencies above 1,000 Hz

findings.antecedent: Larger air gap thickness (B4, 30 cm) vs smaller air gap (B3, 2.5 cm) for WPC Type B
findings.mechanism: Panel absorbers demonstrate superior sound absorption with larger air gap thicknesses.
findings.quote: the comparison of B3 and B4 indicated that the panel absorbers demonstrated superior sound absorption with larger air gap thicknesses

findings.antecedent: Jacobaea maritima garden modules (substrate depth 0.06 m)
findings.mechanism: Lower substrate depth compared to previous studies leads to lower αs with low-frequency sounds, as greater weight and thickness absorb more energy.
findings.quote: the substrate depth used in the present study was less than that used in the studies listed in Table 3. Therefore, that the garden modules in this study displayed lower αs with low-frequency sounds was reasonable

findings.antecedent: Jacobaea maritima garden modules (87.72 plants/m²)
findings.mechanism: Plant density influences overall sound absorption.
findings.quote: the number of plants per square meter employed in the present study was between those in the studies of Davis et al. [23] and Azkorra et al. [25]

findings.antecedent: Jacobaea maritima garden modules (substrate inserted in plastic pots, less exposed)
findings.mechanism: Less exposed substrate reduces sound wave access and energy absorption.
findings.quote: The lower absorption compared with that recorded by Davis et al. [23] was likely a result of the thinner substrate layer and less substrate exposure.

findings.antecedent: Jacobaea maritima plants (tortuosity and softness)
findings.mechanism: Surface tortuosity and softness offer favorable noise reduction properties.
findings.quote: because of its surface's tortuosity and softness, J. maritima was expected to offer favorable noise reduction properties

findings.antecedent: Jacobaea maritima plants (morphology and size)
findings.mechanism: Comparable performance to Boston ferns (broad, dense crowns, irregular leaves) but requiring less space.
findings.quote: J. maritima exhibited potential for noise reduction, with its performance comparable to that of Boston ferns while also requiring less space.

findings.antecedent: Integration of WPC SS (A1 or B1) with 100% Jacobaea maritima garden modules
findings.mechanism: SSs improve sound absorption, especially for low-mid-range frequencies.
findings.quote: The integration of the A1 and B1 SSs improved the sound absorption of the garden modules, as illustrated in Fig. 8.

findings.antecedent: LWS with WPC Type A SS (A2, 2.5 cm air gap, 100% greenery)
findings.mechanism: Combining greenery systems with well-designed SSs can produce a sound absorber for the full range of sound frequencies.
findings.quote: A1 and A2 displayed results similar to those without garden modules, except that A2 had similar or even superior performance to A1 at frequencies above 2,000 Hz.

findings.antecedent: LWS with WPC Type A SS (A6, porous design, 100% greenery)
findings.mechanism: Perforated design complements the greenery system by compensating for its sound absorption deficiencies at low frequencies.
findings.quote: the sound absorption of the LWS improved significantly at frequencies under 500 Hz, and although the performance of A6 at higher frequencies was still inferior to that of A1, the disparity between the two groups was slight.

findings.antecedent: LWS with WPC Type A SS (A1, 100% greenery) vs LWS with WPC Type B SS (B1, 100% greenery)
findings.mechanism: Structural weight is the main factor influencing sound absorption coefficients of LWSs.
findings.quote: the comparison of A1 and B1 showed that the results were similar to those obtained without garden modules, suggesting that the main factor influencing the sound absorption coefficients of LWSs is the structural weight.

findings.antecedent: LWS with WPC Type B SS (B4, 30 cm air gap, 100% greenery) vs LWS with WPC Type B SS (B3, 2.5 cm air gap, 100% greenery)
findings.mechanism: Sound energy at high frequencies is subjected to interference caused by the greenery system's increased reflection, scattering, and tremor mechanism with shorter distances to the ground.
findings.quote: the comparison of B3 and B4 indicated that except for frequencies under 125 Hz, B3 and B4 exhibited similar sound absorption performance until exceeding frequency over 2,500 Hz.

findings.antecedent: LWS with Helmholtz resonator mechanism (A6, B4, 100% greenery)
findings.mechanism: Helmholtz resonator mechanism is more efficient in improving sound absorption at frequencies under 500 Hz.
findings.quote: Helmholtz resonator mechanism might be more efficient in improving sound absorption at frequencies under 500 Hz.

findings.antecedent: LWS with WPC Type B SS (B4, larger air gap, 100% greenery)
findings.mechanism: Panel absorbent with larger air gap could lead to a complex effect of overall morphology including structure and weight.
findings.quote: The behavior of B4 at frequency range over 800 Hz was possibly due to enhanced greenery system vibration caused by SS structure

findings.antecedent: Increased garden module coverage (0% to 100%) on A6 SS design
findings.mechanism: Increased coverage improves sound absorption across octave bands, particularly mid-high frequencies.
findings.quote: as the garden module coverage increased, the sound absorption at all octave bands improved, exhibiting the greatest effectiveness with mid-high frequencies.

findings.antecedent: Increased garden module coverage (0% to 100%) on B4 SS design
findings.mechanism: Combined interaction of structure and weight leads to a decrease in sound absorption at high frequencies with 100% coverage.
findings.quote: Fig. 11 showed a similar pattern (with sound absorption increasing with the increase in garden module coverage), but a noteworthy decrease in sound absorption occurred at frequencies above 2,500 Hz with 100% garden module coverage.

findings.antecedent: Increased greenery coverage (0% to 100%)
findings.quote: The results listed in Table 5 also suggested that the effectiveness of NRC decreased as greenery coverage increased.

findings.antecedent: Greenery coverage less than 65% (A6 SS design)
findings.quote: for less than 65% greenery coverage, A6 exhibited superior performance

findings.antecedent: Greenery coverage 100% (B4 SS design)
findings.quote: whereas the B4 design was superior when combined with 100% greenery coverage.

findings.antecedent: Approximately 33% greenery coverage (this study)
findings.mechanism: Achieving certain sound absorption levels does not necessitate dense greenery coverage and can be performed at a low cost.
findings.quote: a greenery coverage of approximately 33% in this study was associated with similar performance to that in the study of Azkorra et al. [25].

findings.antecedent: LWS-SS designs (A6 and B4)
findings.mechanism: Different designs excel at different frequency ranges, except around 1,000 Hz due to the greenery system's natural feature.
findings.quote: the A6 and B4 SS designs show that various designs excel in sound attenuation at different frequency ranges, except for frequencies of approximately 1,000 Hz

findings.antecedent: Coverage pattern of garden modules
findings.mechanism: The coverage pattern influences sound reflection; variables like the gap between plants could be explored to reduce unnecessary sound reflection.
findings.quote: the coverage pattern of garden modules exerts a certain influence; variables such as the gap between each plant could be further explored to reduce unnecessary sound reflection.

findings.antecedent: Uncovered portions of LWS (natural facades)
findings.mechanism: Natural facades provide a positive impression, and designs balancing visible patterns and greenery offer balanced aesthetic experience.
findings.quote: the uncovered portions of the LWSs developed in this study (with natural facades) may provide a positive impression to pedestrians

mechanisms: Chambers within WPC panels contribute to sound absorption.
Air gaps influence sound absorption based on frequency.
Perforation designs, consistent with Helmholtz resonator and standing wave tube theories, affect absorption frequency range.
Specimen weight is a dominant factor for panel absorber mechanism at low frequencies.
Grooved surface patterns enhance sound scatter, diffraction, and reflection at higher frequencies.
Larger air gap thicknesses improve sound absorption for panel absorbers.
Substrate depth and exposure influence sound absorption, particularly at low frequencies.
Plant morphology, size, tortuosity, and softness contribute to noise reduction.
Integration of support systems with greenery systems improves overall sound absorption, especially at low-mid frequencies.
Helmholtz resonator mechanism is efficient for improving sound absorption at frequencies under 500 Hz.
Greenery system vibration can be enhanced by SS structure, especially with larger air gaps.
Increased greenery coverage generally improves sound absorption, but can lead to complex interactions with structure and weight at high frequencies.
Coverage patterns and gaps between plants influence sound reflection.
Natural facades provide positive aesthetic impressions.
implementation_implications: SS should be carefully considered when designing LWS to optimize effectiveness.
WPC with molding flexibility can help LWS adapt to diverse topographies.
Full greenery coverage is potentially unnecessary; slightly less coverage can be more cost-effective while maintaining aesthetic charm and considerable sound absorption.
Tailoring LWS designs to specific noise sources, local climate, topography, space consumption, and cost constraints is possible.
Utilizing WPC's molding flexibility for convenient irrigation systems, easy assembly, and recycling features can further enhance LWS benefits.
Balancing visible patterns and greenery coverage in LWS designs can offer low overall costs and a balanced aesthetic experience.

Average absorption coefficients of LWSs (100% plant module coverage) with various SSs for sounds at various frequencies (Full range, Low, Medium, High, NRC)

Interaction among LWS design factors (Greenery system: Species, Substrate, Plants/m², Coverage rate; SS: Structure, Surface pattern, Panel Absorbent, Perforation design)

limitations: Further study is necessary to create a function for the absorption of the double-layered panel absorber.
Further research on the influence of perforation might be required for a comprehensive understanding.
The actual weight of front and back panels was hard to measure due to difficulties in fine separation of the boards.
The limited effects of the panel absorber on the sound absorption of the LWS could be better understood through further investigation.
Variables such as the gap between each plant could be further explored to reduce unnecessary sound reflection.
The study did not directly measure human psychological or physiological responses, only acoustic performance.
